html:
These days, alongside my research, I’m researching how to get out of research. Why leave? Here are my reasons (I’ve answered this under another question, too):

  1. Instability. Until you land a tenure-track position, everything is uncertain. Lots of people go from one postdoc to the next, spending years of their lives holding out for a professorship that perhaps fewer than 1% will get. So we see more and more “eternal postdocs” (Chinese slang calls them “thousand-year-old PhDs”), wave after wave of them, defending their professional faith as researchers and scholars. Of course, some people genuinely love research. They can do without hobbies, without a social life, without a family life, even without a life at all, because research is everything to them: the way, the truth and the life. These are born scientists, and it would be a waste for them to do anything else. But many more people probably treat research as an ordinary job that puts food on the table, nothing more. It’s just that the road isn’t as easy as it used to be. A PhD coming home from abroad? Twenty years ago you were the cream of the crop; ten years ago you walked into a faculty job. Now? Just someone. And it’s not only like this in China; Europe is the same. My current boss was born in 1980. After five years as an assistant professor, he got tenure last year and was promoted to associate professor, so he bought a house, had a baby and is now sprinting down the academic road. Among the people I know, there are also some who left for industry after a few years as assistant professors, for reasons unknown. Maybe they couldn’t take it any more, maybe they weren’t considered qualified enough and the university let them go. Several of my PhD friends keep moving from one postdoc to another, building experience, cranking out papers, rushing all over the place, all in pursuit of the top of the ivory tower.
  2. Low pay. This may be what brings every researcher to tears. In China, PhD students get only a token stipend. In North America it’s somewhat better (I haven’t actually looked into it). In Europe, PhD salaries are higher still: you can support yourself and even put some money aside. And after the PhD? Those of us who stayed in academia have already been left behind on salary by the classmates and friends who went into industry. Even with a faculty position the pay isn’t especially high, and it doesn’t match the effort and years you’ve put in. In China, an established professor may do much better, because salary isn’t the only income and may be only a small part of the total: they can start companies on the side or take on industry-funded projects. In Europe, some professors start their own companies too, but most just draw a fixed salary without much on top.
  3. No sense of achievement and no motivation. If there is a motivation in day-to-day academic work, for a professor it’s probably papers and proposals, and for everyone else it’s papers. As the saying goes, papers are everything. Daily life consists of coming up with ideas, writing papers and battling reviewers. Academic fanatics love it. One of the guys I play ball with posts on WeChat every day, and 80% of it is research results, notes on papers he’s read and his email exchanges with reviewers (the other 20% is his kids). Most people rack their brains for something novel, agonize over every word for fear of upsetting a reviewer, and call the reviewer an idiot when the comments come back, day after day, year after year. Over time you set off on a surreal journey of “Who am I? Where am I? What am I doing?” A while ago I came across a remarkably sharp phrase from an American who talks PhDs out of academia, and it sums up the feeling exactly: no milestones of advancements (Cheeky Scientist | Industry Training For Post-Academia PhDs, if you’re interested). When research has so little to do with industry and real life, it easily ends up like Kong Yiji, the pedant in Lu Xun’s story, showing off that he knows four ways to write the same character: it looks impressive, but it’s useless. I’m not dismissing research and scholarship; it’s just that most people are only along for the ride.
  4. Work and life can’t be separated. In Europe, people make a point of keeping work and life strictly apart: work hard during working hours, and enjoy life once you clock off. Academia is the exception. Few people get through a weekend without thinking about a paper deadline, how to phrase a sentence in a manuscript, why the reviewer is being such a bitch, when they’ll finish, where to do the next postdoc, what the proposal should focus on, blah blah. In China, pressure from bosses and the general environment mean even more evening and weekend work: 996, nine to nine, six days a week. Over time, your physical and mental health take a serious hit.
